title: A Journey Beyond Blindness
description: A personal narrative about traveling independently from the United States to the Philippines and building a new life.
author: Kaeleb Savon Heck
paragraphs: I was born blind because of Leber congenital amaurosis, a condition that caused me to grow up experiencing the world differently from most people. Being blind has never meant that I did not have goals, though. For years, people questioned what I could do independently and sometimes assumed that my disability should limit where I could travel or how I could live. One of the biggest moments that challenged those assumptions began on August 21, 2024, when I traveled from the United States to the Philippines by myself. I was not making a short trip. I was traveling across the world to finally meet Emma, the woman I had known and talked with for six years.

My mother took me to Jacksonville International Airport in Florida. I was so excited that I actually wanted to be dropped off the night before my flight. I spent the night sitting on a bench, using my phone and talking with Emma. I was not sitting there thinking about everything that could go wrong. I was thinking about where I was going and about finally turning something that had existed through phone calls and messages into real life. The next morning, airport staff assisted me through the airport while I traveled with my white cane. I boarded my first flight from Jacksonville to Atlanta and arrived at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, where I had a layover of several hours.

From Atlanta, I boarded the long flight to Seoul, South Korea. It was the longest part of the journey, but I was still excited. When I arrived at Incheon International Airport, I became determined to get a South Korean passport stamp. I asked for assistance getting through immigration so that I could officially enter the country during my layover. After getting the stamp I wanted, I returned to the airport and ate at Lotteria, a Korean fast-food restaurant. That might seem like a small detail, but to me it represented something bigger. I was thousands of miles from home, blind and traveling independently, and I was experiencing a country I had never visited before.

Later, I boarded my flight from Seoul to Manila. When I arrived in the Philippines around midnight, the trip suddenly became much more difficult. Immigration officials questioned me closely about why I had come to the country and about my relationship with Emma. Because I was blind, they seemed concerned that someone might take advantage of me. They asked questions about our relationship and wanted to examine information on my phone. At the time, I cooperated because I wanted to enter the country and continue my journey. I had known Emma for six years, and I knew why I had traveled there. Still, I spent hours at the airport waiting while my situation was reviewed.

By about five in the morning, I was finally able to continue. I took another flight from Manila to Davao City. After arriving in Davao, I received assistance getting into a taxi and went to Hotel Sogo, where I finally slept. A few hours later, Emma arrived. After six years of phone calls and messages, we were finally standing in the same place. We were both overwhelmed and cried when we met. That moment made every flight, layover, immigration question, and hour of waiting worth it.

What began as a trip became a completely different life. I decided to remain in the Philippines. About a month later, I traveled to Cebu City to work on documents needed for marriage. On October 8, 2024, Emma and I were married in Kapalong. I later went through the immigration process to establish residency in the Philippines. Our life continued to grow, and on June 24, 2026, our daughter, Madeline, was born.

The most important part of this journey is not simply that I traveled to another country. It is what the journey proved to me. People had told me that I would never make it to the Philippines. Some said Emma was only a “phone girlfriend” or that she was using me. Others saw my blindness and assumed that traveling independently across several countries was beyond what I could safely do. Their predictions did not become my reality.

Being blind does create challenges, and I do use assistance when I need it. Independence does not mean refusing help. To me, independence means making my own decisions, pursuing my own goals, and finding a way forward when something is difficult. On August 21, 2024, I left the United States carrying a white cane, a phone, a passport, and a belief that the life I wanted was possible. That journey eventually led to a marriage, a family, and a new home. It taught me that disability can change how I accomplish something without deciding whether I am allowed to accomplish it.

I used ChatGPT Voice by OpenAI as an accessibility tool to narrate my personal experiences and to receive assistance organizing and editing this personal narrative. The events, experiences, opinions, and reflections described in the narrative are my own.

title: Building a Career in Music: The Work Behind Mr. Blindbandit
description: A researched look at the creative, technical and business work behind a professional independent music career.
author: Kaeleb Savon Heck
paragraphs: A finished song may last only a few minutes, but a career in music is built from hundreds of hours that listeners never hear. Behind every release are decisions about writing, recording, editing, promotion, technology, contracts, scheduling, and audience development. That combination is what attracts me to the career I am already building as Mr. Blindbandit, an independent musician, producer, digital creator, and founder of Blindbandit Records. Being born completely blind has shaped how I work, but it has not reduced the size of the career I want. Instead, it has pushed me to learn accessible technology and to treat sound as both an art form and a practical way of understanding the world. A professional music career fits my interests because it combines creativity, independence, technology, and entrepreneurship; succeeding in it requires continuous training, disciplined daily work, strong promotion, and the ability to adapt to an industry in which income and opportunities can change quickly.

The public usually sees the most visible part of a musician's job: the performance or finished recording. The actual work is much broader. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics explains that musicians perform for audiences and recordings, practice, rehearse, book venues, and promote themselves through websites, social media, interviews, and other publicity (Bureau of Labor Statistics). O*NET adds tasks such as learning new music, participating in studio recordings, arranging music, collaborating with managers, and promoting music through media activities (O*NET OnLine). For an independent artist, many of these responsibilities fall on the same person. A normal week can include developing a song, recording, reviewing mixes, communicating with collaborators, updating a website, planning a release, answering business messages, and posting content. Running Blindbandit Records adds another layer because a label involves organizing projects and building a professional identity. My official press page describes my work as music, production, video, and digital storytelling, showing why I view this career as more than simply performing songs (Mr. Blindbandit).

There is no single educational route into professional music. The Bureau of Labor Statistics states that musicians and singers typically do not need a formal postsecondary credential, although classical and opera performers may pursue bachelor's or advanced degrees. Across genres, however, extensive training and regular practice are essential; business courses such as marketing can also help because self-promotion is part of the profession (Bureau of Labor Statistics). O*NET shows the same mixture of artistic and practical abilities. Its profile lists active listening, speaking, monitoring, reading comprehension, and critical thinking among important skills, while the work requires creativity, planning, accuracy, and cooperation (O*NET OnLine). For me, training is not limited to a classroom. I learn by creating, experimenting with production tools, studying how releases are presented, working with others, and improving the systems I use to manage my music. Formal education can be valuable, but learning continues long after any course ends. I would especially benefit from targeted study in music production, copyright basics, marketing, accounting, and artist management. Those subjects would strengthen the parts of the career that are easy to overlook when the focus stays only on creativity. The more I understand the business behind a release, the better prepared I am to make decisions for both my own work and Blindbandit Records.

Accessibility is a major part of my training. I was born blind with Leber congenital amaurosis, so I do not work by looking at visual waveforms or watching a screen. I use screen readers, audio feedback, keyboard commands, memory, and careful listening to move through digital tools. On my website, I describe the difference simply: "What other people look at, I listen to" (Heck). Some software is built around visual controls, which can require a different workflow; at the same time, relying on sound has made close listening central to how I create. My press materials explain that I use accessible technology and screen readers while working across ambient, cinematic, electronic, and hip-hop sounds (Mr. Blindbandit). Accessibility is therefore not separate from my career. It shapes how I organize files, operate software, communicate online, evaluate sound, and solve problems. Learning to work independently with accessible tools is part of my professional training.

The financial side of a music career is less predictable than a traditional salary. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median hourly wage of $47.80 for musicians and singers in May 2025, but nearly half of workers in the occupation were self-employed, and federal wage data do not include the self-employed. Part-time and intermittent work is also common (Bureau of Labor Statistics). The median figure therefore should not be read as a guaranteed full-time income. Independent musicians may earn from several activities instead of one steady paycheck. The job outlook is competitive as well: employment is projected to show little or no overall change from 2025 to 2035, although about 17,400 openings are expected each year as workers leave the occupation or move into other jobs (Bureau of Labor Statistics). These numbers show why creativity must be matched with discipline, promotion, financial planning, and the willingness to create multiple opportunities.

Location can influence opportunities, but technology has changed what location means for an independent artist. The Bureau of Labor Statistics notes that musicians perform in concert halls, clubs, churches, studios, and other settings and may travel locally, nationally, or internationally (Bureau of Labor Statistics). A performer may benefit from living near an active music market or network of venues. My own career also shows how digital work can cross borders. I have roots in Virginia and now live in the Philippines, while Mr. Blindbandit and Blindbandit Records maintain an online presence that can reach beyond one city or country (Mr. Blindbandit). Geography still matters because of time zones, travel costs, and local networks; however, websites, digital distribution, online communication, and remote collaboration make it possible to build parts of a music career from almost anywhere. That flexibility allows my creative work to continue while I build a life in the Philippines.

My experiences are another reason music feels like the right career. Blindness has required me to ask questions, learn unfamiliar systems, and solve practical problems without depending on sight. Those habits are useful in an independent creative business. In August 2024, I traveled alone from the United States to the Philippines, moving through multiple airports with my white cane, screen-reader technology, and assistance when I needed it. I later wrote that I did not confuse independence with pretending I never needed help (Heck). That lesson applies directly to music. An independent artist still needs collaborators, listeners, distributors, technicians, and other professionals; independence means being responsible for the direction of the work, not refusing support. Sound has always carried information for me - voices, movement, distance, emotion, rhythm, and space - so turning sound into creative work connects naturally to skills I have developed throughout my life. Mr. Blindbandit represents a career path built around how I already think, listen, communicate, and create.

I do not romanticize the profession. The Bureau of Labor Statistics identifies dedication, discipline, interpersonal skills, musical talent, stamina, and promotional skills as important qualities for musicians and singers (Bureau of Labor Statistics). Those qualities connect to everyday realities: rejection happens, schedules can be irregular, audiences have endless choices, and an artist may spend as much time promoting a release as creating it. O*NET also emphasizes organization, relationships, problem solving, and keeping knowledge current (O*NET OnLine). I want to keep strengthening those areas by improving my production skills, learning more about the business side of music, building professional relationships, maintaining an accessible website, and treating releases as organized projects. Talent may attract attention, but a sustainable career depends on habits and systems that continue when excitement fades. The creative side and the business side have to work together; ignoring either one makes the career harder to maintain.

A career in music is demanding because it asks one person to be creative, technical, organized, persistent, and public at the same time. Research from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and O*NET shows that musicians must do far more than perform: they practice, record, promote, collaborate, travel, plan, and continually develop their skills. The field does not require one universal degree, but it does require serious training, and its income can be irregular even for skilled professionals. For me, those challenges do not make the career less attractive. They make it a career worth approaching deliberately. My experience as a blind creator has taught me to adapt tools to my needs, to listen closely, and to keep moving when a process is difficult; my work as Mr. Blindbandit and founder of Blindbandit Records gives those abilities a professional direction. I want a career that allows me to create sound, tell stories, build something of my own, and connect with people across borders. Music does all four, which is why it is not only a career I am interested in someday - it is the career I am already learning how to build.

title: The Best Post-Secondary Path Is the One That Fits the Student
description: An argument for choosing education and training that fits each student’s goals, abilities, accessibility needs and finances.
author: Kaeleb Savon Heck
paragraphs: For generations, students have often heard one basic message after high school: go to college if you want to be successful. College can absolutely be the right choice, but it is not the only path to a meaningful career. Students have different abilities, financial situations, interests, disabilities, and goals. Some careers require a four-year degree, while others can be reached through community college, technical training, apprenticeships, entrepreneurship, or direct work experience. The best post-secondary path for students is therefore not one universal route. Students should choose the education or training that matches their career goals, strengths, accessibility needs, and financial circumstances.

There is strong evidence that higher education can provide major economic benefits. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, workers age twenty-five and older with a bachelor’s degree had median weekly earnings of $1,578 in 2025, compared with $966 for workers whose highest credential was a high school diploma. The unemployment rate was also lower for bachelor’s degree holders, 2.8 percent compared with 4.3 percent for high school graduates (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Education Pays”). These numbers are an important argument for college, especially for students pursuing careers that require degrees. A student who wants to become a teacher, engineer, attorney, or physician cannot simply replace the required education with ambition.

However, those statistics do not prove that every student needs the same type of education. The Bureau of Labor Statistics itself separates occupations according to different entry-level requirements, including associate degrees, post-secondary nondegree awards, high school diplomas, and other forms of training (“Employment, Wages”). The U.S. Department of Education also recognizes career pathways that include career and technical education and apprenticeships (“Career Pathways”). These options matter because success should be measured by whether a person gains the skills needed for a chosen career, not by whether everyone earns the same credential.

My own life is one reason I believe this. I was born blind because of Leber congenital amaurosis, and throughout my life people have sometimes assumed that blindness should determine what I can do. I learned the opposite. In 2024, I traveled independently from the United States to the Philippines, using my white cane and airport assistance when necessary. That experience reinforced something I had already learned through music: independence does not mean doing everything in exactly the same way as everyone else. It means finding the tools and pathway that allow you to reach your goal.

Music became one of my pathways. I developed my identity as the artist Mr. Blindbandit and built Blindbandit Records. I have also worked on developing my online presence through MrBlindbandit.net. My path has required creativity, technology, communication, persistence, and learning how the music business works. It has not looked like a traditional four-year college route, but that does not make the skills or work less real. For a blind student, accessibility can also influence which route makes sense. A program may look excellent on paper but become a poor choice if its technology, materials, or training environment is inaccessible. Students with disabilities should be able to consider accessibility as part of choosing a path without being told that their disability makes their ambitions unrealistic.

Critics might argue that encouraging alternatives to four-year college could cause students to settle for less. That concern deserves attention because education is strongly associated with higher earnings and lower unemployment. Yet giving students more choices is not the same as discouraging education. In fact, it requires students to think more carefully about what education they actually need. A future nurse may need a nursing degree, while another student may benefit more from an apprenticeship, a technical credential, an associate degree, or specialized business training. The Department of Education describes career exploration as a way for students to connect their interests and abilities with education and training options, including non-college programs (“Career and Educational Pathways”). The goal should be informed choice rather than automatic enrollment.

Cost also makes this decision important. Spending years in a program that does not connect to a student’s goals can waste both time and money. Students should compare tuition, potential debt, accessibility, expected earnings, job opportunities, and the actual qualifications employers require. The right answer may still be a university degree, but it should be chosen for a reason. For someone else, a shorter credential or work-based program may provide a faster and more practical route into a career.

There is no single post-secondary path that guarantees success. College remains valuable and necessary for many careers, but it should be one option among several respected choices. My experience as a blind person, musician, entrepreneur, and international traveler has taught me that a person’s path does not have to resemble everyone else’s to be legitimate. Students need accurate information, accessible opportunities, and the freedom to choose a route that fits their goals. The best path after high school is not simply the path people traditionally expect. It is the path that gives an individual student the strongest realistic opportunity to build the life and career that student wants.
